translations.text: I can tell a true story about myself, tell of my journeys: how in days of toil I often suffered times of hardship, and have endured bitter sorrow of heart,
have known many places of sorrow aboard ship, the terrible rolling of the waves, where the anxious night-watch often took hold of me at the ship's prow as it tossed along the cliffs.
My feet were pinched by cold, bound by frost in cold fetters, while cares sighed hot around my heart; hunger within tore at the spirit of the sea-weary man.

that the man to whom things fall out most pleasantly on earth does not know how I, wretched and full of care, spent the winter on the ice-cold sea on the paths of exile, cut off from my dear kinsmen, hung about with icicles; hail flew in showers.

There I heard nothing but the roaring sea, the ice-cold wave. At times I took the song of the swan as my entertainment, the cry of the gannet and the call of the curlew in place of men's laughter, the singing gull in place of mead-drinking.
Storms beat the stone cliffs there, and the icy-feathered tern answered them; very often the dewy-feathered eagle screamed around them. No protecting kinsman could comfort the desolate spirit.
So the man who has known the joy of life in the towns, and few hard journeys, proud and flushed with wine, can hardly believe how I, weary, often had to wait out my time on the sea-path.
The shadow of night grew dark, snow came from the north, frost bound the ground, hail fell on the earth, the coldest of grains.

And so the thoughts of my heart now press on me to try for myself the high streams, the tossing of the salt waves. Again and again my mind's desire urges my spirit to set out, so that far from here I may seek the land of foreigners.
For there is no man on earth so proud in spirit, nor so generous with his gifts, nor so bold in his youth,
nor so brave in his deeds, nor with a lord so gracious to him, that he never has anxiety about his seafaring, about what the Lord will do with him.

His mind is not on the harp nor on receiving rings, he takes no joy in a woman and has no hope in the world, nor in anything else except the rolling of the waves; but the one who sets out on the sea always feels longing.

The groves break into blossom, the towns grow fair, the fields grow beautiful, the world hurries on; all these urge the eager mind and spirit to the journey, in one who intends to travel far on the paths of the sea.

Likewise the cuckoo urges him with a mournful voice; the guardian of summer sings, and foretells sorrow, bitter in the heart. The man blessed with comfort does not know what some endure who travel the paths of exile most widely.
So now my thought roams beyond the enclosure of my breast; my spirit roams widely with the sea-flood over the whale's home,
over the expanses of the earth, and comes back to me eager and greedy; the lone flier cries out and urges my heart irresistibly onto the whale's way, over the expanse of the seas.
For the joys of the Lord are warmer to me than this dead life, fleeting on land. I do not believe that earthly riches will last forever.
Always, in every case, one of three things becomes a threat before a man's hour comes: sickness or old age or the sword's hatred will wrest the life from the doomed man as he departs.
And so for every man the praise of the living who speak of him afterward is the best memorial: that before he must go on his way he should work, by good deeds on earth against the malice of fiends,
by brave deeds against the devil, so that the children of men may praise him afterward, and his praise may then live with the angels for ever and ever, the glory of eternal life, joy among the hosts.

The days are gone, and all the pomp of the kingdom of earth. There are now no kings or emperors or gold-givers such as there once were, when they did the greatest glorious deeds among themselves and lived in the most lordly renown.
This whole noble company has fallen, and the joys are gone. The weaker ones remain and hold this world, and enjoy it through toil.
Glory is brought low. The nobility of the earth grows old and withers, as every man now does throughout the world.
Old age comes upon him, his face grows pale; the grey-haired man mourns, knowing that his friends of former days, the children of nobles, have been given to the earth.
Then, when life leaves it, his body cannot swallow anything sweet or feel pain, nor stir a hand nor think with the mind.

Though a brother may strew his brother's grave with gold, and bury him among the dead with all kinds of treasures that he wants to go with him, gold cannot help a soul full of sins in the face of the terror of God, if he hoards it beforehand while he lives here.
Great is the terror of the Creator, before which the earth will turn aside; he established the firm foundations, the expanses of the earth and the heaven above.
Foolish is the man who does not fear his Lord; death comes to him unexpected.
Blessed is the man who lives humbly; grace comes to him from heaven. The Creator makes his mind steadfast, because he believes in His might.
A man must steer a strong mind and keep it firm on its foundations, and be true to his word with men, pure in his ways. Every man should keep moderation toward friend and toward foe [?] malice,
[?] though he may wish to [?] him full of fire, or burned up on the pyre, his friend whom he has made. Fate is stronger, and the Measurer mightier, than any man's thought.

Let us consider where we have a home, and then think how we may come there, and then let us also strive to be allowed to enter into the eternal blessedness, where life depends on the love of the Lord, and hope is in the heavens.
Thanks be to the Holy One for this, that he has honoured us, the Prince of glory, the eternal Lord, for all time. Amen.
